planting.note: Divide and plant in early spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; tolerates drier shade once established.

directions: Set divisions in spring at the base of shrubs or along the edge of a woodland bed where soil drains well but is not kept constantly wet. This stoloniferous relative of sweet woodruff spreads steadily by creeping underground stems into a dense weed-suppressing mat of whorled green leaves topped by clusters of small tubular white to pale pink flowers in late spring. Unlike its sweeter-scented cousin, it tolerates calcareous and summer-dry soils, making it useful under deciduous trees where moisture is seasonal. Cut back tired foliage after flowering to encourage fresh regrowth and keep the mat tidy.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, well-drained woodland soil with consistent moisture in part sun to light shade.

directions: Plant in dappled light under high deciduous canopy where the soil stays evenly moist and rich in organic matter. Each spring, upright fleshy stalks emerge bearing two or more whorls of broad, glossy olive-green leaves, and by April the stalk tips carry short pendent racemes of tiny, strongly fragrant white flowers that hang beneath the foliage. The clump dies back to the rootstock in winter and slowly widens into an architecturally distinct colony among other woodland perennials. Avoid heavy summer shade that stunts flowering, and mulch with leaf litter to protect the shallow rhizomes over winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Site in a cool, shaded woodland bed with steady moisture and deep organic mulch, since stems rise taller than most Chloranthus and benefit from shelter against wind. Strong rhizomes send up erect, clearly jointed stems whose leaves clasp the stem without a stalk, crowding near the tip into a whorled rosette above bare lower nodes. In March and April the stem tips produce slender terminal spikes with pendulous side branches of small white flowers, followed by fruit through early summer. Divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigor and propagate new plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil in partial to full shade; resents summer heat and drought.

directions: Grow this close relative of Ypsilandra thibetica in cool, shaded, consistently moist woodland soil enriched with leaf mold. Evergreen rosettes of narrow strap-shaped leaves send up slender flowering scapes bearing a long bottlebrush-like spike of small, fragrant white flowers over many weeks from April into June, more floriferous per spike than its better-known relative. It spreads slowly into a tidy colony at the front of a shaded path or rock garden and rarely needs division except to propagate. Keep roots cool with a steady leaf-litter mulch and avoid any site that dries out or bakes in direct sun.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist, acidic soil in deep partial to full shade.

directions: Tuck divisions into shaded, humus-rich pockets of a woodland or rock garden where moisture stays constant through the growing season. This diminutive evergreen rosette-former from the hill forests of southern China sends up short nodding spikes of small, fragrant tubular flowers that vary from white to soft pink or purple depending on the wild-collected form. It forms a low, slow-spreading mat of narrow, glossy foliage useful as a textural accent among taller woodlanders rather than as broad groundcover. Because stock is still uncommon outside specialist collections, start with a single division and increase it gradually rather than splitting hard in the first few seasons.
